extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, FDA/regulatory counsel, judges, and parties litigating Orange Book listing disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for when a patent may be listed in the FDA’s Orange Book for an NDA product—focusing on the statutory meaning of “claims the drug,” the role of active ingredients, and how patent-claiming differs from infringement. Useful for evaluating listability/delisting counterclaims under Hatch‑Waxman/FDCA provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'claims the drug' for Orange Book listing
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent "claims the drug for which the applicant submitted the application" when the patent "particularly points out and distinctly claims" the drug as the invention (35 U.S.C. §112(b)); it is not satisfied merely because an NDA product would infringe a patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court rejects equating ‘‘claims’’ with ‘‘reads on’’ or mere infringement. To decide whether a patent claims the drug, analyze the patent document (claims and specification) to see whether the inventor defined the invention as the drug or drug constituent at issue. Examples/authority: 35 U.S.C. §112(b); Phillips v. AWH; Hoechst‑Roussel; the opinion contrasts claiming (internal document-based inquiry) with infringement (external-product-based inquiry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing requires both 'claims the drug' and that infringement could reasonably be asserted
rubrics_metrics.description: The listing provision includes two distinct statutory requirements: (1) that the patent "claims the drug for which the applicant submitted the application" and (2) that "a claim of patent infringement could reasonably be asserted" (21 U.S.C. §355(b)(1)(A)(viii) and related provisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as separate conditions; interpreting them as coterminous would render statutory language redundant. Evidence of (possible) infringement alone does not satisfy the separate statutory requirement that the patent claims the drug. The court relies on textualist canons to give effect to both elements (citing Reiter v. Sonotone and Nat’l Assn of Mfrs. v. Dep’t of Defense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent must claim at least the active ingredient to be listable
rubrics_metrics.description: To be listed in the Orange Book, a patent must claim an invention that contains at least the active ingredient identified in the NDA; patents claiming only device components or other non‑active parts of the approved product do not meet the listing requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule follows from the FDCA statutory scheme and FDA approval practices: drug approval centrally focuses on the active ingredient; ANDA applicants must have the same active ingredient (21 U.S.C. §355(j)(2)(A)(ii)); cases cited include Sandoz and Ipsen. Policy rationale: the active ingredient is what makes a product approvable as a drug; listing a patent that does not claim the active ingredient would assert patents outside the scope Congress intended for Orange Book listing. Practical anti‑pattern: attempting to list patents that claim only dose counters, canisters, or other device parts of an NDA product is improper under this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'drug' in FDCA by examining statutory context, not an isolated clause
rubrics_metrics.description: The FDCA’s broad textual definitions (e.g., components intended for use in treating disease) must be read in the broader statutory and regulatory context that distinguishes drugs from devices and that centers drug‑approval on active ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on the clause defining a drug as an article intended to treat disease or as a component; consider other FDCA provisions, the separate device regulatory regime (21 U.S.C. §321(h)), combination‑product provisions, and FDA approval pathways. The court cites Brown & Williamson and Genus Med. to justify harmonizing provisions so the meaning of "drug" reflects the FDA’s regulatory scheme. Practical effect: not every component of an NDA combination product is a "drug" for listing purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between claiming (claim construction) and infringement (literal + doctrine of equivalents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming focuses on what the patent document (claims and specification) particularly and distinctly claims (inquiry guided by Phillips), while infringement asks whether a particular accused product contains each claim limitation (literal infringement) or is equivalent (doctrine of equivalents) under 35 U.S.C. §271(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing listability, use claim‑construction principles (intrinsic evidence, prosecution history, extrinsic evidence per Phillips) to determine what the patent claims. Recognize that infringement doctrines (literal reading vs. equivalents) are separate theories; infringement can be shown in ways that do not change what the patent actually claims. Examples: Allen Eng’g on literal infringement; Warner‑Jenkinson and Wilson Sporting Goods on doctrine of equivalents; Hoechst‑Roussel and Apotex discussed to distinguish the inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are defined by the patent document and specification (35 U.S.C. §112 and Federal Circuit precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is a numbered paragraph that particularly points out and distinctly claims the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention (35 U.S.C. §112(b)), and the specification must describe and enable that invention (35 U.S.C. §112(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of whether a patent 'claims' a drug requires reading the claims together with the specification to define the invention the patentee sought to protect. The court cites Phillips, Merrill v. Yeomans, and the statutory enabling/written description mandates to support this inquiry. Practical implication: a claim that focuses on a device component need not enable or describe the whole NDA product (e.g., a steering wheel claim need not describe the entire car).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination‑product designation and NDA approval do not automatically make device components listable as the 'drug'
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the FDA approves a combination product via an NDA (because the primary mode of action is that of a drug), that administrative designation does not convert device components into listable "drug" inventions unless the patent claims the active ingredient or invention that made the product approvable as a drug.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 21 U.S.C. §353(g), the FDA uses primary mode of action to determine which center/approval pathway applies. But statutory and regulatory treatment of combination products does not alter the Orange Book’s statutory requirement that a patent claim the drug (i.e., the active ingredient). The court rejects Teva’s argument that combination‑product FDA processing means patents to device parts are listable. Cite to SMDA and Genus Med. for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statutory interpretation canons in listing disputes (avoid redundancy; give words effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting listing/delisting provisions, courts must give effect to each statutory term and avoid interpretations that render statutory language meaningless or redundant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion applies canons (Reiter; Nat’l Assn. of Mfrs.) to reject interpretations that collapse distinct statutory requirements (e.g., 'claims' vs 'infringement'). Practitioners should craft arguments that respect separate statutory elements and explain how proposed readings fit the FDCA/Hatch‑Waxman scheme as a coherent whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent requiring focus on what the patentee claimed, not merely what an approved product might contain or metabolize into
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior case law (e.g., Hoechst‑Roussel) holds that a patent claiming a particular compound does not necessarily 'claim' a chemically distinct compound administered in the approved product, even if the claimed compound results from metabolism of the administered compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these precedents to argue that metabolic products or impurities that may be present or produced by the approved product do not make a patent listable unless the patent itself claims the administered active ingredient. Example: Hoechst‑Roussel's treatment of 1‑hydroxy‑tacrine vs tacrine hydrochloride; Sandoz on impurities; Ipsen on classifying by active ingredient.
